cross.h: Plans look more alike than different
cross.t: In every region, people-first strategies are 30 to 45% of the latest national plan and growth strategies 30 to 48%. Apart from natural capital in Egypt's plan, no framework family sits more than about 4 points above or below the all-country average. Regions differ in what they lean toward, not in the shape of the tree.

cross.h: Climate is the storm almost every region names
cross.t: Climate change is the risk tied to the most strategies in six of the eight regions, ahead of every other risk in the Pacific (17% of strategies) and South Asia (16%). Europe and Central Asia is the exception: pandemics lead there (14%). In the Arab States, environmental degradation and resource pressures tie with climate. Yet the climate framework family itself is only about 5% of strategies on average, so the risk is named more often than it is answered.

cross.h: Plans act through organisations, rarely through money
cross.t: Almost half of all strategies (47%) work through organisations: programmes, agencies and capacity. Another 28% work through information and 18% through rules. Only 8% use money, such as grants, subsidies or tax measures, and in the Pacific just 4%. Spending choices show up in budgets, not in the plans.

Only about a quarter of strategies (24%) carry a quantified target, and fewer than one in five (18%) name how they will be monitored. South Asia comes highest on targets (34%), while Latin America and the Caribbean (13%) and the Arab States (14%) come lowest. This holds back the RHDR Making Change Happen pillar across the board.

South-East Asia.h: Growth through knowledge, clusters and upgrading
b: Knowledge (7.7% against 6.6%), linkages, clusters and cities (6.3% against 5.2%) and upgrading and innovation (5.7% against 4.8%) sit above the average. The region builds its growth on skills and industrial depth.
Climate change is the risk named most (16% of strategies), but the climate family is below average (3.7% against 4.7%), and so is health (4.0% against 4.9%).
Across seven countries' plan series, later plans put less on domestic integration (down 2 points) and future generations (down 2 points), and more on broad governance and people goals.

South Asia.h: The most specific plans, leaning to skills, trade and accountable government
b: South Asian plans are the easiest to place: 67% of strategies reach a lever (62% on average), and 34% carry a quantified target (24% on average).
They lean to knowledge, reaching foreign markets, accountability and authorised flexibility (7 of 9 countries above the average). They put less on enterprise finance and market rules.
Across seven plan series, delivery capability is rising (up about 2 points) and domestic integration is falling (down about 3 points).

East Asia.h: Growth-first plans: upgrading, cities and infrastructure
b: Growth strategies make up 43% of the latest plans (35% on average). Upgrading and innovation (9.0% against 4.8%), linkages, clusters and cities (8.9% against 5.2%) and infrastructure (5.9% against 4.3%) stand out.
Technological change is a leading risk alongside climate (11% of strategies). Authorised flexibility and rapid resource mobilisation are light, in both countries.
There are two countries here. China and Mongolia each count for half.

Pacific.h: Plans for protection and stewardship, less for export growth
b: Future generations, the subpillar holding climate, natural capital and resilience, is larger than in any region except the Arab States (16% of strategies against 12%). Climate is above the average in 7 of 10 countries.
Market rules and property rights (above average in 9 of 10 countries) and economic and human wealth (8 of 10) also stand out, because land and resource tenure runs through Pacific plans.
Export-led growth is half the average (4% against 8%), upgrading and innovation is light (2.7% against 4.8%), and only 4% of strategies use money as the instrument.

Europe and Central Asia.h: Competitiveness and market access, with pandemics as the storm
b: Growth strategies make up 48% of the latest plans, the highest of any region. Infrastructure and connectivity (7.7% against 4.3%), enterprise and finance (6.3% against 3.7%) and reaching foreign markets (4.9% against 2.4%) lead.
Pandemics are the most-named risk (14% of strategies). This reflects Serbia's plan for 2021 to 2023.
Only two countries are read here, Kazakhstan and Serbia. Uzbekistan's plan yields too few strategies to count.

Arab States.h: Resource stewardship and broad economic goals
b: Natural capital is twice the average (12.4% against 6.2%), and environmental degradation, resource pressures and climate are the leading risks (14 to 15% each).
Broad economic goals that fit no family are large (12.4%), and governance is light (5.2% against 10%).
This reads as Egypt's Vision 2030 alone. Morocco's document yields too few strategies to count, so treat this as a country note, not a regional message.

Africa.h: Living standards, trade and data, with fewer transformative strategies
b: Decent standard of living (8.3% against 6.7%), reaching foreign markets (3.5% against 2.4%) and data sharing (2.3% against 1.1%) lean above the average, the last two in 4 of 5 countries.
Natural capital (4.5% against 6.2%) and authorised flexibility are light. Fewer strategies are framed as transformative than anywhere except the Arab States (17% against 22%).
Five countries are read here: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Rwanda. Only national plans and some budgets are in, with no sector plans or UNGA statements.

Latin America and the Caribbean.h: The most people-first plans, aimed at exclusion and places
b: People-first strategies make up 45% of the latest plans, the highest of any region. Tackling structural exclusion is more than double the average (9% against 4%), and spaces and decent standard of living are above the average in all four countries.
Knowledge is the lightest of any region (4.2% against 6.6%, no country above the average).
The fewest strategies are tied to a risk (27% against 36%), and the fewest carry a quantified target (13%). Brazil's plan is the hardest to place: 39% of its strategies reach a lever.
